stories.title: The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season
stories.summary: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory The Pacific’s Busy Storm Season Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search Tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific Basin has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam, and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October. When the EPIC (Earth Polychromatic Imaging Camera) on the DSCOVR (Deep Space Climate Observatory) satellite captured this image (above) on October 29, 2026, Super Typhoon In-fa churned near the Mariana Islands. At the same time, the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea. In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year. The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured the image of In-fa below on October 30, when the storm was just west of the island chain. In-fa was unusually intense at the time of the image, with a nearly circular shape and large eye—a collection of characteristics that meteorologists use to identify a subset of tropical cyclones known as annular storms . These storms typically lack prominent outer spiral-shaped rainbands—a common feature of standard tropical cyclones—which is why meteorologists have a habit of calling annular storms “doughnuts” or “truck tires.” Annular storms are rare, accounting for just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, according to one analysis . Their eyes average about 45 kilometers (30 miles) in diameter, compared to about 25 kilometers for standard tropical cyclones, and the storms typically maintain their strength longer in unfavorable conditions. In-fa was still a tropical cyclone when EPIC captured the image at the top of the page, but Champi’s leftovers had gone through the process of extratropical transition and become a whole different type of storm as they entered the Bering Sea’s busy storm track. Tropical cyclones are warm-core storms fueled by the heat and moisture of warm ocean water, but extratropical cyclones typically have cold cores and draw energy from temperature contrasts between warm and cold air masses. Unlike tropical cyclones, extratropical cyclones typically develop fronts and huge, spiraling cloud bands shaped like commas . “One of the calling cards of extratropical transitions is the expansion of a storm’s wind field,” said Gary Partyka, a meteorologist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “It’s not that the winds necessarily grow stronger, but they cover a much larger area,” he said. In this case, there likely would still have been a midlatitude storm over the Bering Sea, possibly with large, comma-shaped clouds on October 30, even without Champi’s remnants, he added. “But it looks like Champi became intertwined with and helped intensify that system,” he said. Champi’s transformation came after a long and destructive tour through the West Pacific, during which the typhoon achieved maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometers (185 miles) per hour, prompting some observers to call it one of the strongest storms of the season. Despite narrowly skirting Taiwan and Guam, the powerhouse storm brought damaging winds and intense rains to both places, as well as to parts of China and Japan. When the remnants hit Alaska, the state avoided catastrophic damage on the scale of what happened after ex-typhoon Halong struck in October 2025 , but some areas did see high winds and heavy rain and snowfall, according to news reports . Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, noted University of Alaska Fairbanks meteorologist and climatologist Rick Thoman , following Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September, and Choi-wan in early October. The autumns of 1997 and 2015—both very strong El Niño years—had three each, he added. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have impacted the state since 1970 , according to Thoman. Partyka described 2026 as a “particularly active year” for Pacific tropical cyclones, increasing the chances that Alaska would be affected by storms that have gone through extratropical transitions. The strong El Niño underway in the Pacific is a “likely contributor” to the increased activity, he added. El Niño is a climate pattern that emerges roughly every two to seven years, marked by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. In the Northwest Pacific, the phenomenon tends to cause storms to more readily curve northward rather than continuing westward to East Asia and Southeast Asia, some experts say , bringing more storms toward Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, Japan, and the Korean Peninsula. stories.title: Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now
stories.summary: 6 Min Read Happy 65 Years: NASA’s Johnson Space Center Then and Now View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Sixty-five years ago, a bold vision took root in Houston: a NASA center dedicated to human spaceflight. Since its founding, NASA’s Johnson Space Center has helped lead the nation’s human spaceflight program, supporting missions from Project Mercury through Artemis. Today, Johnson serves as NASA’s Center of Excellence for Human Spaceflight, and its workforce is helping to usher in a Golden Age of innovation and discovery. Johnson is home to America’s astronaut corps, the Mission Control Center, and the teams behind some of humanity’s greatest achievements in space. As NASA’s human spaceflight programs evolve, Johnson remains at the forefront of these efforts. Houston is home to NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, comprising International Space Station operations and commercial partnerships and destinations in low Earth orbit. For missions beyond low Earth orbit, Johnson houses the Moon Base Program⁠ and Orion Program⁠ , while NASA’s Human Health and Performance Directorate⁠ and Human Research Program ⁠ work to protect crew health and performance as missions extend farther from Earth. On May 25, 1961, the center’s story began when President John F. Kennedy gave a speech before a joint session of Congress, committing the nation to achieve the goal of landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before the end of the decade. NASA’s Space Task Group, in charge of America’s human spaceflight program, was already working on Project Mercury to put astronauts into Earth orbit, but with the additional task of a human lunar landing, it soon outgrew its facilities at NASA’s Langley Research Center in Hampton, Virginia. The agency decided it needed a dedicated field center for human spaceflight and on Sept. 19, 1961, after evaluating multiple sites around the country, NASA announced that the new Manned Spacecraft Center would be built near Houston, Texas. The agency established the center on Nov. 1, 1961, and construction began in 1962. In 1973, it officially became NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in honor of President Johnson for his ardent support of America’s space program from its foundation. Manned Spacecraft Center to Johnson Space Center The Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, and while construction continued on the Clear Lake site, employees worked in 13 leased buildings in southeast Houston. The design phase took six months and construction of the first buildings took 18 months, with the first employees moving onto the new site in late 1963. Over the decades, the number of buildings grew, and continues to grow, to meet the demands of new spaceflight programs. View of the Manned Spacecraft Center during construction in 1963. Aerial view of NASA’s Johnson Space Center and Space Center Houston in 2025. NASA/James Blair Project Management Building Construction of the nine-story Project Management Building began on Dec. 5, 1962, and concluded on March 15, 1964. Robert Gilruth , the center’s first director, moved into his office on March 5, 1964, on the top floor of the edifice then known as Building 2. The building swapped numbers with the Public Affairs Building, originally known as Building 1, on June 30, 1974. The main administration building, called Building 2 until 1974, during President Richard Nixon’s visit in 1974. Employees pose for a group photo in front of Building 1 in 2024. NASA/Robert Markowitz Photo taken in 1964 from the main administration building toward the city of Nassau Bay. The same view from roughly the same vantage point in 2026, showing the mature oak trees and the extensive development outside the center’s gates. Neutral buoyancy spacewalk training The use of neutral buoyancy for spacewalk training began with the Gemini XII mission in 1966. In 1967, workers installed an above-ground circular pool called the Water Immersion Facility for astronaut training that supported Apollo and pre-Shuttle spacewalk training.. To accommodate the larger size of the space shuttle payload bay, spacewalk training moved to the Weightless Environment Training Facility iin 1980. Astronauts used it for nearly all shuttle spacewalk training until 1997, when the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory in the Sonny Carter Training Center entered operations for both shuttle and space station training, as well as testing future space suits and lunar surface activities. Astronaut candidate Anna L. Fisher trains at the Water Immersion Facility in Houston in 1979. Exploration geologists and Artemis science officers Trevor Graff, left, and Angela Garcia carry out a lunar training development run at NASA’s Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory (NBL) in Houston. This testing run marked the first time in the Artemis program that two geologists were suited up simultaneously for lunar geology training in the NBL. Lunar Receiving Laboratory (Building 37) To prevent any back contamination from any possible lunar microorganisms, NASA designed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in Building 37. Construction began in August 1966, with the first employees moving into their offices in June 1967. The astronauts from Apollo 11, 12, and 14 completed their three-week postflight quarantine in the lab, and scientists in the various laboratories studied the lunar samples all the Apollo missions returned. Following the Apollo program, Life Sciences division and laboratories moved into the building until they relocated in 2017. Following demolition of Building 37, the Lunar Receiving Park, dedicated in 2026, honors the history of the laboratory. Building 37 that housed the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in May 1969, two months before the first Moon landing. Aerial view of the Lunar Receiving Park built on the site of Building 37 in 2026. NASA/Robert Markowitz A scientist views an Apollo 11 Moon rock at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory in 1969. Spacecraft mockup training facilities (Building 9) Construction of Building 9 began in December 1965 and finished in March 1967. The building initially housed the Technical Services Facility. In April 1969, workers converted a portion of the building to include a mock lunar surface scene, complete with a mockup of a Lunar Module, used by Apollo 11 astronauts. To support the space shuttle program, workers completed an addition that housed the Mockup and Integration Laboratory in September 1974. Astronauts for all 135 shuttle missions used the mockups for training. An extension on the northwest side of thebuilding begun in 1986 and completed in 1988. It received mockups of Space Station Freedom and later of the International Space Station, and the building was renamed the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility. Today, the facility also houses training mockups of NASA’s Orion spacecraft, commercial mockups, and the Active Response Gravity Offload System, known as ARGOS. Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong, left, and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin train for their lunar spacewalk in Building 9 in April 1969. The Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026 NASA/Robert Markowitz Apollo 13 astronaut Fred Haise trains for his lunar spacewalk in Building 29 using the six-degrees of freedom simulator in January 1970. In the Space Vehicle Mockup Facility in Building 9 in 2026, NASA astronaut Nicole Mann evaluates a new spacesuit design using the Active Response Gravity Offload System, or ARGOS. NASA/David DeHoyos Mission Simulation and Training Facility (Building 5) Construction of Building 5 , the Mission Simulation and Training Facility completed inApril 1965 and began supporting missions beginning with Gemini IV in June 1965. The building originally contained the Gemini spacecraft simulator and a Gemini translation and docking simulator. Apollo program simulators, including a command module and lunar module simulator, began arriving in December 1965. From 1967 and 1978, astronauts used the Water Immersion Facility for spacewalk training. In the early 1970s, the building also housed full-scale, high-fidelity trainers and simulators of Skylab’s components, which all nine Skylab astronauts used for mission training. In the late 1970s, the facility underwent major renovations to support the space shuttle program, with the addition of fixed base and motion base simulators. The Space Station Training Facility addition, completed in 1991, supported first Space Station Freedom and now International Space Station crew training, and also contains Orion and Starliner simulators. The Gemini Translation and Docking Simulator in Building 5 in March 1965 used for astronauts to train on docking with Agena target vehicles. NASA astronauts Stephanie Wilson, left, Jonny Kim, and Randy Bresnik inspect the Orion spacecraft simulator in Building 5 in 2022. stories.title: TB 26-09 Measured Hammer-Tap Inputs
stories.summary: For more information, contact Joel W. Sills, Langley Research Center, joel.w.sills@nasa.gov . Download the PDF version An instrumented hammer test does not require an idealized single half-sine waveform. When the complete force and response are measured accurately, crest ripples and separated contacts remain known inputs. Force shape changes excitation, but does not inherently invalidate the record. Adequacy depends on measurement accuracy, bandwidth, signal-to-noise ratio, and coverage of the test objective. Background: What the Hammer Actually Measures Hammer tests support modal analysis [2–4] and can precede pyroshock testing [6]. Figure 1 compares a half-sine, maintained-contact rippling, and separated contacts. During a zero-force interval, the structure continues to vibrate; re-contact acts on that vibration. If an exact model and test article receive the same force and initial conditions, uniqueness gives identical responses for each bounded measured history. An approximate model can show different errors as inputs excite different frequencies, amplitudes, or nonlinear states. See [1] for the exact-model derivation. Analysis: A Half-Sine Is Broadband, but Not Flat Figure 2 shows that a finite half-sine is broadband but contains spectral zeros at f/fo = 3, 5, 7, …, with fo = 1/(2T) for pulse duration T. Its appearance alone cannot establish adequate excitation. Analysis: Spectral Content Is Determined by the Measured Force History Figure 3 normalizes each spectrum to its own DC value. Crest rippling adds content and can fill half-sine notches. Timing between separated contacts creates deterministic interference. For adequacy, inspect the unnormalized measured spectrum and response signal-to-noise ratio. Recommended Practice: Evaluate Test Adequacy Against the Intended Objective • Measure the complete applied force with adequate bandwidth, calibration, dynamic range, and time synchronization. • Verify that the response measurements have adequate bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio and are not clipped or saturated. • Confirm that the excitation covers the frequency, amplitude, and nonlinear-response ranges required by the intended test objective. • Reject or repeat a test only for an identified measurement, excitation, or coverage deficiency. Conclusion Half-sine appearance neither establishes validity nor guarantees adequacy. Judge each hammer test by its purpose and by accurate, complete force and response measurements over the required range. References 1. A. Majed, J. Sills, E. Henkel, V. Babuska, S. Yunis, D. Hamilton, J. Akers, and T. Kinney, Validity and Predictability of Measured Hammer Tap Inputs: Linear and Nonlinear Structural Systems, September 2026. 2. D. J. Ewins, Modal Testing: Theory, Practice and Application, 2nd ed., 2000. 3. ISO 7626-5:2019, Mechanical Vibration and Shock—Experimental Determination of Mechanical Mobility—Part 5 4. K. G. McConnell and P. S. Varoto, Vibration Testing: Theory and Practice, 2nd ed., 2008. 5. A. H. Nayfeh and D. T. Mook, Nonlinear Oscillations, 1979. 6. NASA-STD-7003, Pyroshock Test Criteria, 1999

stories.title: Week Starts with Spacewalk Preps and Life Science
stories.summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon points his camera toward his spacesuit’s helmet visor and takes an out-of-this-world “space selfie” during a pscewalk on Oct. 29, 2026. NASA Editors note: This blog was updated on Nov. 2 to reflect an update in coverage and spacewalk start times. Preparations continue for the second in the final series of spacewalks to upgrade the International Space Station ’s power generation system on Thursday. Meanwhile, the Expedition 75 crew focused its research efforts on life science at the beginning of the week. Flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Anil Menon of NASA will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array during a spacewalk planned to start at 7 a.m. EST on Thursday. The duo will work on the orbital outpost’s starboard truss structure opposite from the port truss structure where they installed a roll-out solar array on Oct. 29 . Upon completion of the installation job, which is expected to take about seven hours, the station’s power generating capacity will increase about 30 percent from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. NASA+ begins its live spacewalk coverage at 5:30 a.m. on Thursday and also will stream on a variety of other platforms. Kutryk and Menon joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney on Monday and studied the Canadarm2 robotic arm procedures necessary to support Thursday’s spacewalk. The quartet also called down to mission controllers for a pair of pre-spacewalk conferences. The astronauts first discussed their mission readiness with spacewalk specialists then spoke to robotics engineers afterward about any Canadarm2 concerns. Microgravity research was still on Monday’s schedule for the astronauts as they helped researchers advance human health on Earth and in space. Kutryk strapped on the Bio-Monitor ’s sensor-packed vest and headband at the beginning of his shift and pedaled on the Destiny laboratory module ’s exercise cycle . Results may show how an astronaut’s cardiorespiratory system adapts to weightlessness informing crew health measures on future missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Delaney nourished growing vascular tissues samples that were printed inside the BioFabrication Facility . Watkins verified the operation of a portable DNA sequencer used to genetically analyze antibiotic-resistant bacteria in microgravity. Expedition 75’s three cosmonauts stayed focused on their task list of space research and lab maintenance inside the orbiting complex’s Roscosmos segment. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov continued studying how to manufacture high-purity semiconductor crystals in microgravity that are superior to those produced on Earth. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov attached electrodes to himself for a 24-hour session measuring his heart activity and blood pressure. Flight engineer Anna Kikina worked on ventilation system maintenance then worked on cargo transfers inside the Progress 96 cargo spacecraft . stories.title: What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA
stories.summary: Skywatching Skywatching Home What’s Up Meteor Showers Eclipses Daily Moon Guide More Tips & Guides Skywatching FAQ Night Sky Network Meteor Showers, a Spacecraft Milestone, and a Supermoon Catch Taurid and Leonid meteors, spot Mars near Jupiter, celebrate Voyager 1’s light-day milestone, and watch November’s supermoon. Skywatching Highlights Around Nov. 5: Southern Taurids peak; occasional bright fireballs Around Nov. 12: Northern Taurids peak; around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 15-16: Mars and Jupiter appear 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise Nov. 17: Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation Nov. 17-18: Leonids before dawn after moonset; up to around 15 meteors per hour under ideal conditions Nov. 24: Full supermoon; first in a series of three consecutive supermoons A full Moon rises over Vasquez Rocks Natural Area and Nature Center north of Los Angeles, California, on June 24, 2021. Credit: NASA/Preston Dyches Transcript A month of meteor showers … a close pairing of Mars and Jupiter … and a supermoon! That’s What’s Up for November. November offers a buffet of opportunities to see a meteor streak across the sky! The Southern Taurids peak around November 5th, followed by the Northern Taurids around November 12th. Those names refer to the two areas in the constellation Taurus, where the meteors appear to originate. Each Taurid shower produces only a handful of meteors per hour—around five, under ideal conditions—but an occasional bright fireball can make the wait worthwhile. A sky chart showing where to look for the Leonids in November 2026. NASA/JPL-Caltech Next up are the Leonids. For the best viewing times, try the early morning hours of November 17th and 18th, after the Moon sets. Under ideal conditions, the shower could produce around 15 meteors per hour, though most viewers will see fewer. To level up your viewing experience, you will want to find a dark location, give your eyes about half an hour to adjust, and take in as much sky as you can. Around mid-month, there’s another reason to head outside early. On the mornings of November 15th and 16th, look southeast before sunrise to see Mars and Jupiter close together. A sky chart showing Mars and Jupiter close in the night sky. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech They’ll appear about 1.2 degrees apart—a little more than the width of two full Moons side by side. Jupiter is the brighter point of light, with reddish Mars nearby. Both planets are easy to see with the unaided eye. They’re still far apart in space, but from Earth, they appear almost side by side. Watch over several mornings to see them draw closer together – and then go their separate ways. Artist’s rendering of a NASA Voyager spacecraft traveling through interstellar space. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech This month, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft will reach a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth. That means a signal traveling at the speed of light takes 24 hours to reach the spacecraft – and another 24 hours for us to hear back from it! If you want to imagine where Voyager 1 is currently traveling, look in the direction of the constellation Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer. A night sky chart highlights the location of Voyager 1 within the constellation Ophiuchus on November 17 around 5 p.m., looking toward the western horizon. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech And on November 17th, join us in celebrating this milestone by participating in our Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day activation. Learn more at nasa.gov/voyager . On November 24th, the evening sky will be lit by a supermoon. Because the Moon’s orbit is slightly oval, its distance from Earth changes. When it’s closer, the full Moon appears larger and brighter than average – though the difference can be subtle. This kicks off a series of three consecutive supermoons in November, December, and January. Look east around sunset to watch it rise. It may look even bigger near the horizon, but that’s the Moon illusion —a common effect with any full Moon. Here are the phases of the Moon for November: Moon phases for November 2026, showing the dates for Third Quarter, New Moon, First Quarter, Full “Supermoon,” and a concluding Third Quarter in Pacific Time. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech You can stay up to date on all of NASA’s missions exploring the solar system and beyond at NASA Science . I’m Raquel Villanueva from NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and that’s What’s Up this month. stories.title: NASA Invites Media to Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Station Resupply Launch
stories.summary: Northrop Grumman’s Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft is pictured on Oct. 9, 2026, in the grip of the Canadarm2 robotic arm moments before its release into Earth orbit after a nearly six‑month stay attached to the International Space Station’s Unity module. The orbital outpost was soaring 263 miles above the Indian Ocean, off the coast of Madagascar, at the time of this photograph. Credit: NASA Media accreditation is open for the next launch to deliver NASA science investigations, supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station. A Northrop Grumman Cygnus XL spacecraft will launch in November to the orbital laboratory on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket for NASA. The mission is known as NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25, or NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25. Liftoff is targeted for no earlier than 10:49 a.m. EST, Sunday, Nov. 29, from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following launch, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 robotic arm to capture Cygnus and install the spacecraft to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading. The spacecraft will remain at the space station until May 2027. This is the company’s 25th spacecraft built to deliver supplies to the International Space Station under contract with NASA. Credentialing to cover prelaunch and launch activities is open to U.S. media. The application deadline for U.S. citizens is 11:59 p.m. EST, Thursday, Nov. 12. All accreditation requests must be submitted online at: https://media.ksc.nasa.gov Credentialed media will receive a confirmation email following approval. NASA’s media accreditation policy is available online. For questions about accreditation, or to request special logistical support, email: ksc-media-accreditat@mail.nasa.gov. For other questions, please contact NASA’s Kennedy Space Center newsroom at: 321-867-2468. In addition to food, supplies, and equipment for the crew, Cygnus will deliver several new experiments, including hardware to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles in space that could improve drug delivery for cancer and osteoarthritis, as well as a study that could guide cancer treatments by predicting whether a patient’s cancer is likely to spread to other parts of the body. Cygnus also will carry human muscle cells and medications to test therapeutics for muscle loss associated with spaceflight and aging on Earth, and a compact radiation sensor designed to improve crew safety on future missions. Each resupply mission to the station delivers scientific investigations in the areas of biology and biotechnology, Earth and space science, physical sciences, and technology development and demonstrations. Cargo resupply from U.S. companies ensures a national capability to deliver scientific research to the space station, increasing NASA’s ability to conduct new investigations aboard humanity’s laboratory in space. For 26 years, people have lived and worked continuously aboard the International Space Station, advancing scientific knowledge and making research breakthroughs that are not possible on Earth. The space station is an important testbed for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of long-duration spaceflight and to expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. As commercial companies concentrate on providing human space transportation services and destinations as part of a strong low Earth orbit economy , NASA is focusing its resources on deep space missions to the Moon as part of the Artemis and Moon Base programs to build on our foundation for the first astronaut missions to Mars. Researchers found that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by their stars. Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage–ESA/Hubble Collaboration, Alessandra Aloisi (STScI, ESA) NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope just revealed a mystery in our cosmic neighborhood. In a paper published Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using Hubble studied 37 nearby dwarf galaxies — small galaxies containing a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars — and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. Simulations predict that significantly more oxygen, a tracer of a wider set of heavy elements, should reside in these galaxies. So where did it go? “Oxygen is produced by stars, which are inside of galaxies. We know that the oxygen had to be inside of the galaxies at some point in the past, so the oxygen must have been ejected,” said co-investigator Grace Telford, assistant professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Utah. “And to do that, you need energy from massive stars and supernova explosions to drive material out of the host galaxies and into the space between galaxies.” Galactic winds unleashed by supernovae are apparently more effective at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current models predict, according to the new study. The findings show that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by stars. This is an image from NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope of NGC 4449, one of the dwarf galaxies in the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) study. Researchers found that dwarf galaxies can hold onto only a small fraction of the oxygen made by their stars. Image: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage–ESA/Hubble Collaboration, Alessandra Aloisi (STScI, ESA) In the Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds (GLOW) project, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation, scientists traced the oxygen to understand how it is distributed inside stars, in the gas between stars, and in the space between galaxies. But, of all the elements in the galaxies, why study oxygen? Oxygen, the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium, is relatively easy to detect and measure, and its production is well understood — making it a reliable indicator of how chemical elements are distributed in a galaxy. “So, it’s really for practical reasons that we’ve chosen oxygen,” said Kristen Wingfield McQuinn, GLOW principal investigator and mission head of the Science Operations Center for NASA’s newly launched, panoramic Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, Maryland. She also is an associate professor at Rutgers University in New Brunswick, New Jersey. “Oxygen is one of the primary elements formed by stars. Being able to trace how much oxygen gets made, and then how much is distributed inside and outside of galaxies, helps us understand galaxy evolution,” said McQuinn. “It also helps us learn where and how much galaxies are enriching the space between galaxies, called the intergalactic medium.” The study used archival optical imaging data from Hubble to resolve stellar populations and determine star-formation histories and compositions. Along with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope as well as the ground-based Very Large Array and Australian Telescope Compact Array, the researchers analyzed 37 nearby dwarf galaxies to trace oxygen atoms produced by stars. The team wanted to understand how oxygen is distributed across the stars, gas, and dust in the galaxies. These dwarf galaxies were selected because their masses fall in the range where simulations and theory predict that an increasing amount of their oxygen will be expelled from the galaxies via supernovae explosions. These 37 galaxies also are all close enough for Hubble to resolve their individual stars. That’s not true for the vast majority of known dwarf galaxies, which are too far away for this kind of study. Although astronomers already suspected that galaxies expel a large fraction of oxygen and other heavy elements, an open question has been where these metals end up. A previous study from 2014 addressed this question for Milky Way-like, star-forming galaxies, finding that these galaxies lost a large fraction of their oxygen, some of which is found in the diffuse haloes of gas surrounding galaxies outside their disks, called the circumgalactic medium. In the GLOW study, McQuinn and her team extended this research to low-mass galaxies across a wide range of masses and environments. While previous teams have measured oxygen in the circumgalactic medium of dwarf galaxies, it is still unclear if most of the missing oxygen is in this region, or if it has been completely ejected from the galaxy’s surroundings. In the future, McQuinn hopes to study even lower-mass galaxies in the nearby universe. She has an approved program to use the Roman Space Telescope to find these faint and tiny systems across a wide swath of sky. Once she’s identified these galaxies, McQuinn hopes to use Hubble and NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope to get deeper observations of their stars. This would allow her to reconstruct the galaxies’ histories to understand how they formed stars across cosmic time. Telford’s future work involves using Hubble to zoom in on the individual, massive stars that produce oxygen and eject it from their host galaxies. She’s using some of the nearby GLOW targets to get very detailed observations to characterize how the massive stars are different in these small galaxies. The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for over three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA. A Long Cloud on Mars Explanation: What’s causing this unusually long cloud on Mars ? Known as the Arsia Mons Elongated Cloud (AMEC) and first recorded by NASA’s Viking Orbiter 2 in 1977, the strange cloud has been imaged in greater detail more recently by ESA ’s robotic Mars Express spacecraft. The featured image is from 2018. The cloud forms only during spring and summer seasons and then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causes cloud crystals to form around bits of dust would fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in the Martian atmosphere . Leading speculation holds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcano Arsia Mons , wind blows the cloud downstream — creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understand AMEC s will continue, an understanding that may bolster a more complete view of cloud formation on Earth . stories.title: Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon
stories.summary: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search October 25, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison North-central Pennsylvania is canyon country with an Appalachian flair. Pine Creek Gorge reaches depths of about 1,500 feet (460 meters) along its gently curving path through the forests of the Allegheny Plateau . Instead of the steep rock walls characteristic of canyons in the desert Southwest, lushly vegetated slopes outline the dramatic topography. In autumn, greens give way to a palette of reds and golds sought out by leaf peepers. Nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania,” the gorge runs for some 45 miles (72 kilometers) from Ansonia south to Pine Creek’s confluence with the West Branch Susquehanna River, reaching its greatest depths around Waterville. The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 8 satellite captured this image of Pine Creek Gorge on October 25, 2026, when colorful fall foliage was on display. Glaciers played a key role in the canyon’s formation, though ice itself did not carve it. Pine Creek once flowed to the north , opposite of what it does today. As glaciers advanced into the region from the northeast during the last ice age, they dammed the river and filled the valley with lakes. Those lakes eventually overflowed, sending water streaming to the south. Autumn colors emerge along Pine Creek Gorge in this view from Colton Point State Park on October 11, 2009. fishhawk , via Flickr When the ice receded, Pine Creek was already becoming entrenched in its southward course. Rocks and sand left behind by the melting ice further prevented the water from turning back north. Glacial meltwater continued to rush through the valley, deepening and shaping it into its current form. Today, the hillsides around the gorge are blanketed in northern hardwood and mixed oak forest, sprinkled with hemlock and white pine. In autumn, the deciduous trees impart red and gold hues to the landscape akin to the rock of the famous Arizona canyon . October 9 October 25 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 9 October 25 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison October 9 October 25 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Image Details Foliage in the northern hardwood and oak forests around Pennsylvania’s Pine Creek Gorge takes on fall color between October 9, 2026 (left), and October 25, 2026 (right). The images were acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 . NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison. This seasonal change around Pine Creek Gorge has not always been so visually pleasing. With increasing demand for wood products in early 19th-century America, loggers found their way to the area’s stately trees. At the time, white pine and hemlock several feet in diameter and towering hardwoods populated the slopes around Pine Creek Gorge. The pines were especially valued for making ship masts, and hemlock bark was used to tan leather. Before railroads, logs were floated down Pine Creek to the Susquehanna in massive drives. By the early 20th century, decades of logging left the land so barren that the area earned the moniker “Pennsylvania Desert.” The forest has since returned, and with it, wild inhabitants such as black bears, coyotes, bobcats, timber rattlesnakes, and a diversity of songbirds. In 1968, an area of 30,000 acres (12,000 hectares) was designated a National Natural Landmark . Visitors can experience the gorge’s natural splendor at many points along its path, including from multiple state parks and the Pine Creek Rail Trail . stories.title: Space Crops and Advanced Tech Wrap Up Week Following Spacewalk
stories.summary: Expedition 75 flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) and Jessica Watkins of NASA pose together inside the International Space Station’s Quest airlock during a spacesuit fit check. NASA/Anil Menon Space crops research wrapped up the week following the completion of the first of two power upgrade spacewalks at the International Space Station . The Expedition 75 crew members rounded out their research schedule with virtual reality and super intelligence studies. The orbital outpost has a new roll-out solar array that is generating power after flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) installed it during a spacewalk on Thursday . Menon and Kutryk spent seven hours and 11 minutes in the vacuum of space attaching the roll-out solar array to the port side truss structure then releasing its tension bolts allowing the solar array to unfurl, or roll out, on its own during a ten-minute process. The pair will install one more roll-out solar array on Thursday, Nov. 5, to complete the yearslong process that began in June 2021 to augment the space station’s power generation system. Menon and Kutryk will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array on the starboard side of the truss structure increasing the station’s power generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. Menon and Kutryk had a light duty day on Friday with ongoing research planned for their short schedule. Menon worked on a space botany investigation in the Kibo laboratory module exploring how microgravity affects cell division on green algae and cultured tobacco cells. Results may support the production of food crops on the Moon and Mars. Kutryk pedaled on the European Enhanced Exploration Exercise Device’s (E4D) exercise cycle in the Columbus laboratory module . The compact all-in-one E4D is being tested for its ability to keep crews fit during a long-term spaceflight. NASA flight engineer Luke Delaney also studied space-based crops focusing on how to prevent plant diseases in microgravity. Delaney inoculated thale cress plant samples after they were exposed to a fungal pathogen then stowed the samples inside an artificial gravity-generating incubator . Results may improve crop disease resistance both on Earth and in space. NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins spent her shift servicing a variety of research hardware. She first removed and photographed components inside a device that powers experiments launched aboard spacecraft. Next, Watkins swapped moisture absorbers inside a set of portable science freezers that can be launched to the station and returned back to Earth housing frozen research samples for analysis. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov of Roscosmos worked on a physics experiment swapping hardware inside a temperature-controlled chamber to explore manufacturing high-purity semiconductor crystals in microgravity. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryatnikov wore a virtual reality headset and responded to computerized visual stimuli to testing how his sense of balance and orientation is adapting to microgravity. Flight engineer Anna Kikina studied how super intelligence tools may increase operational and communications efficiency aboard a spacecraft. stories.title: Spacewalkers Install Roll-Out Solar Array for Power Generation
stories.summary: NASA astronaut Anil Menon rides the Canadarm2 robotic arm to begin the installation of a roll-out solar array on the International Space Station’s port-side truss structure while orbiting 260 miles above Earth. NASA+ NASA astronaut Anil Menon and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Joshua Kutryk concluded their spacewalk outside the International Space Station at 3:08 p.m. EDT. During the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk, Menon and Kutryk installed and deployed an International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Array (IROSA) on the station’s 2A electrical power channel. The array is the seventh IROSA installed on the station and will provide additional power to support critical operations, including a safe and controlled deorbit. Menon and Kutryk also completed several get-ahead tasks to prepare for a planned Thursday, Nov. 5 spacewalk, when they will install the eighth and final IROSA on the 3B power channel. NASA will provide live coverage beginning at 6:45 a.m. Learn how to watch: https://www.nasa.gov/live/ Following the Nov. 5 spacewalk, the roll-out solar arrays will be fully installed, completing the space station’s power system augmentation. Together, the eight arrays will increase available power by up to 30%, boosting the station’s power generation capacity from 160 kilowatts to approximately 215 kilowatts. U.S. spacewalk 100 was Menon’s fourth and Kutryk’s first. It also was the 285th spacewalk in support of space station assembly, maintenance, and upgrades. stories.title: Astronauts Are Go For Thursday’s Power Upgrade Spacewalk
stories.summary: From left, Astronauts Anil Menon of NASA and Josha Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) pose for pre-flght crew portraits at Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas. NASA Mission managers have given the go for Thursday’s spacewalk to install a new roll-out solar array on the International Space Station ’s port-side truss structure. Expedition 75 flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) will set their spacesuits to battery power at 8 a.m. EDT signifying the start of their spacewalk for about six hours and 45 minutes of external maintenance. NASA+ begins its live spacewalk coverage at 6:30 a.m. On Thursday, the spacewalking duo will first unbolt the roll-out solar array from a temporary stowage platform. Next, Menon will carry the roll-out solar array to the truss worksite while riding the Canadarm2 robotic arm . Kutryk will the translate to the port truss worksite while tethered to the orbital outpost and join Menon to complete the installation job. Finally, mission controllers will remotely activate the roll-out solar array to begin generating power. Menon and Kutryk began their shift on Wednesday finalizing their spacewalk procedure reviews. Afterward, the pair inspected their spacesuits’ life support systems, communications gear, and other components ensuring their readiness for Thursday’s excursion. After lunchtime, Menon and Kutryk joined NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney for a final spacewalk conference with specialists on the ground. Watkins and Delaney also familiarized themselves with lighting conditions and camera locations on the outside of the space station in order to monitor the spacewalkers and operate the Canadarm2. Finally, all four astronauts gathered at the end of their shift for a conference with robotics engineers to discuss Canadarm2 operations planned for the spacewalk. stories.title: Week Begins with Robotics Prep for Spacewalk and Advanced Research
stories.summary: City lights sparkle across the southern United States in this photograph from the International Space Station is it orbited above Florida. At right, is a set of the orbital outpost’s main solar arrays augmented by a smaller set of roll-out solar arrays. NASA Expedition 75 began the week gearing up for a spacewalk to upgrade the International Space Station ’s power generation system. Research into bioprinted blood vessels and relaxation techniques, as well cargo operations rounded out Monday’s schedule. Flight engineers Anil Menon of NASA and Joshua Kutryk of CSA (Canadian Space Agency) will exit the Quest airlock at 8 a.m. EDT on Thursday to install one of two roll-out solar arrays on the orbital outpost’s port side truss structure. NASA flight engineers Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will support the spacewalkers in and out of their spacesuits and assist the duo with the Canadarm2 robotic arm during the planned six-hour and 45-minute spacewalk. Live coverage of the spacewalk will begin on NASA+ starting at 6:30 a.m. The four astronauts joined each other on Monday and familiarized themselves with the Canadarm2 maneuvers necessary to support Thursday’s spacewalk. Menon and Kutryk will first release the roll-out solar array from an external pallet. Menon then will attach himself to the robotic arm, retrieve the roll-out solar array, then ride the Canadarm2 to the installation worksite. Kutryk will remain tethered to the truss structure, translate to the port truss worksite, and join Menon to complete the installation job. Afterward, mission controllers will activate the new roll-out solar array. Menon and Kutryk also checked out their emergency spacesuit jetpacks for fuel quantity, battery power, and thruster functionality. Watkins then assisted Kutryk ensuring spacesuit cooling and water systems were safely configured for Thursday’s spacewalk. Watkins and Menon also had time to work inside the SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft transferring supplies back and forth from the space station. Dragon docked autonomously to the Harmony module ’s space-facing port on Oct. 15 and is due to return to Earth in mid-November loaded with science and hardware for analysis. Delaney began his shift documenting his sleep patterns on a computer tablet for the RelaxPro investigation that is exploring how to improve stress reduction during a long duration spaceflight. Next, he treated and nourished bioprinted blood vessel tissues helping researchers take advantage of microgravity to create custom, individualized tissues for patients. Station commander Pyotr Dubrov and flight engineer Anna Kikina, both from Roscosmos, partnered together wearing arm, wrist, and finger cuffs to measure the responsiveness of the circulatory system to weightlessness. Flight engineer Sergey Teteryanikov continued studying how super intelligence tools may advance crew operations and communications with mission controllers. The orbital residents also trained to use a pair of robotic arms and set up Earth photography sessions to round out the day in low Earth orbit. A bioprinter, also called the BioFabrication Facility located in the Columbus laboratory module , was in operation aboard the orbital outpost printing blood vessels using vascular cells. stories.title: NASA Completes Artemis III Booster Stacking, Shares Status Update
stories.summary: Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems completed integrating the aerodynamic nose cones onto the left and right forward assemblies on the twin SLS (Space Launch System) solid rocket boosters, finishing their stacking operations for Artemis III inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. Each forward assembly contains an aerodynamic top, a forward skirt housing avionics, and frustum housing motors that allow the boosters to separate from the SLS core stage after launch. The twin solid boosters will help support the remaining rocket components and the Orion spacecraft during final assembly of the Artemis III rocket and provide more than 75 percent of the total SLS thrust during liftoff from NASA Kennedy’s Launch Pad 39B. NASA/Cory S Huston Progress on NASA’s Artemis III’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket continues at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, where teams have completed the integration of the final solid rocket booster motor segments onto the mobile launcher for the “short stack” configuration that will be used during a tanking test. Teams also completed installation of all four RS-25 engines on the SLS core stage. Teams now will install the systems tunnel that runs the length of the core stage and is used to route pyrotechnic cabling, a system of wiring that allows the single-use, quick disconnect for controlled movements during liftoff, on the massive stage. In the coming weeks, the stage will be integrated with the solid rocket boosters, completing the rocket’s “short stack” configuration. NASA will roll the short stack SLS rocket from the spaceport’s Vehicle Assembly Building to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test in the coming months, where the Artemis launch team will practice procedures and timelines for loading propellant. While at the pad, the Artemis III crew, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick, Frank Rubio, Andre Douglas, and ESA (European Space Agency) astronaut Luca Parmitano, also will conduct a launch day rehearsal and emergency exit walkdown. This will include suiting up in astronaut crew quarters, driving to the launch pad, ascending the mobile launcher, and then walking through the exit route they would take in the unlikely event of an emergency during launch countdown. Additional hardware updates At Launch Pad 39B, teams continue the refurbishment of the flame deflector, which saw minimal damage after the Artemis II launch. The bricks on the flame trench itself were not affected by the launch due to ground support improvements informed by lessons learned after Artemis I in 2022. Teams are continuing to work through testing on the Orion spacecraft. Recently, engineers with ESA and Airbus inspected the solar array wings, which deliver power to the service module that provides propulsion, thermal control, and electrical power to the spacecraft, as well as air and water for the crew. Technicians extend and inspect one of the solar array wing panels that will attach the Orion service module for Artemis III inside the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building high bay at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026. Each solar array panel, provided by the European Space Agency and built by Airbus, generates 11 kilowatts of power and spans about 63 feet to supply Orion’s power, propulsion, air, and water through low Earth Orbit. NASA/Amanda Stevenson At NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the forward and aft rings were welded on the Artemis III spacer, completing the primary structure. The spacer will serve to represent upper stage dimensions during the mission. The dimensional checks are underway. Engineers also are converting two existing structural test articles, the Orion stage adapter and launch vehicle stage adapter, into flight-ready hardware. Exterior painting on the Orion stage adapter was recently completed at NASA Marshall, with cables and brackets to be installed soon. The launch vehicle stage adapter has undergone detailed inspection and preparation, with corrosion removal nearly complete, and nondestructive evaluation will begin this fall. Following that evaluation, technicians will apply conversion coating to the interior, prime and paint the exterior, and spray the cone-shaped adapter with thermal protection spray foam. The spacer and both adapters remain on track to ship to Kennedy early next year. Crew training continues The Artemis III crew has continued a variety of training activities to prepare for their mission. Recently, they completed lessons on the flywheel exercise device, practicing hardware setup, anticipated exercises, and equipment disassembly. This compact device, about the size of an extra-large shoe box, uses pulleys and a torque limiter to mimic a rowing machine, allowing aerobic, resistive, and rowing exercises with straps attached to either a bar or harness. Nutrition also is a key focus. At NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory in Houston, crew members sampled nearly 200 items on the menu to select their favorites for the mission, ensuring their health and performance are supported throughout. The Artemis III crew tasted various food items on Monday, Aug. 10, 2026, at NASA’s Space Food Systems Laboratory, to determine what they’ll eat on their mission in low Earth orbit. NASA/Helen Arase Vargas The crew concluded helicopter underwater egress training, practicing escape from a submerged, upside-down mock helicopter cabin in a controlled pool environment to prepare for potential off-nominal water crash-landings. Last week, members of the Artemis III crew traveled to San Diego to participate in recovery training with NASA and military partners, practicing water lifts by U.S. Navy helicopters. They completed several suited training activities in the Orion Crew Survival System Suits this week, preparing for post-insertion, deorbit procedures, and emergency responses. These activities included communication system checks, suit operations, emergency equipment handling, contingency drills, and cabin configuration with stowage, ensuring the crew is ready for any scenario that may arise. The Artemis III astronauts pose for a group photo on the front porch before conducting hoist training with U.S. Navy Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 23 and Explosive Ordnance Disposal Group (EODGRU) 1 in San Diego, California, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. In preparation for NASA’s Artemis III, NASA and the Department of War will conduct training evolutions to demonstrate and evaluate the processes, procedures, and hardware used in recovery operations for crewed lunar missions. US Navy/2nd Class August Clawson In September, the full Artemis III crew and backup astronauts visited Florida together for the first time since their crew announcement earlier this year. The astronauts visited their Orion spacecraft, saw the integrated solid rocket boosters on top of the mobile launcher, and viewed the core stage undergoing final processing ahead of integration. The crew also visited commercial partners SpaceX and Blue Origin to become more oriented with the lunar lander providers’ progress, marking one more milestone in preparation for the daring Artemis III mission. stories.title: NASA Releases Artemis II Lunar Science Data, Images
stories.summary: NASA astronauts Christina Koch (below) and Victor Glover (above) share a window inside the Orion spacecraft during the sixth day of the Artemis II mission. Flight Day 6 was the crew’s lunar flyby day, during which they rotated roles taking photos, making annotations, and recording their scientific observations of the lunar surface. (April 6, 2026) NASA NASA’s Artemis II crew traveled around the Moon and back and, along the way, captured stunning imagery and scientific observations of our nearest neighbor. NASA is making the full lunar science dataset from their journey available Wednesday to the global science community and the public for further study. More than 800 gigabytes of Artemis II lunar science data – some previously unreleased – have been uploaded to NASA’s Planetary Data System, the public archive for NASA’s planetary missions. This data release includes more than 11,000 full-resolution images and video of the Moon from the crew’s handheld cameras and the Orion spacecraft’s cameras, 8.5 hours of audio recordings of the crew’s scientific observations of the lunar surface, and crew-annotated images. When combined, the images, audio files, and crew notes from the expedition provide a powerful lunar science dataset ripe for exploration and analysis. This is the first planetary science dataset captured primarily by humans in more than half a century and humanity’s influence on it is clear. Through training in classrooms, simulations, and field environments, NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, and CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen developed expertise in lunar geography, geology, and observational best practices. Their quick decisions about observation targets and which images to capture, along with their perceptions of color and dynamic changes, and discussions about the science of the lunar surface and its surroundings complement decades of data from Apollo astronauts and robotic explorers and deepen our understanding of the Moon as NASA prepares for long-term exploration of the lunar surface. A screenshot from an Artemis II crew member’s tablet shows handwritten annotations made during the lunar flyby on April 6, 2026, atop a visualization of the dark Moon eclipsing the Sun. Three crew members, who signed their first names, noted impact flashes and their locations on the image. NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Victor “Ike” Glover wrote in blue and green, respectively, while CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen wrote in red. (April 7, 2026) NASA/CSA Along with this data, NASA has released the Artemis II Preliminary Lunar Science Report , the Artemis II Lunar Science Operations Report , and the Artemis II Lunar Science Data User Guide . Together, these three publications provide an overview of the Artemis II lunar mission data and activities, and a technical summary of how the science plan was developed and implemented. This information is already helping inform NASA’s exploration plans for Artemis III and beyond. stories.title: NASA's DAVINCI Probe Can Stand the Heat
